title: Microsoft Purview: sensitivity label protection policies for Azure Blob Storage and Data Lake Storage Gen2
summary: Hold: the permissions guidance omits roles Microsoft requires for policy authors and Azure permissions required to enable enforcement. The documented paths, label-scope command, roadmap facts and combined licensing model are supported, but administrators following the abbreviated permissions instructions could be unable to complete setup.

claims.where: Risk assessment: Data exposure
claims.claim: Data Map auto-labeling conditions do not support custom sensitive info types, trainable classifiers or Exact Data Match.
claims.quote: Custom sensitive info types and advanced classifiers like named entities (All Full Names, All Physical Addresses), trainable classifiers, credentials, and Exact Data Match are not supported.

claims.where: Risk assessment: Security & identity; Governance guidance; rationale: risk
claims.claim: Scan service principals must be included in an allowed security group to prevent later scans being blocked on labeled files.
claims.quote: Ensure that any service principal accounts running data governance scans for the scoped sources are included in a Security Group. Add this Security Group to the allowed list of your protection policies.

claims.where: controls[0].note; Risk assessment: Security & identity; Governance guidance; Governance controls
claims.claim: Policy authors need the Information Protection admin roles plus Data Map reader roles, as the page lists them.
claims.quote: User needs the roles from within the built-in role group “Information Protection”, along with new roles for data map reader, insights reader, scan reader, source reader.
claims.fix: Replace the abbreviated role requirement throughout with: 'Policy authors need the roles in the Information Protection role group plus Data Map Reader, Insights Reader, Scan Reader and Source Reader.' In the Before rollout bullet, say 'Assign the Information Protection role-group roles plus Data Map Reader, Insights Reader, Scan Reader and Source Reader to policy authors.' The existing cited Azure-sources page explicitly requires all four reader roles.

claims.where: controls[1].note
claims.claim: The Azure-sources page names the Data Owner/Admin as the person who enables a source for enforcement.
claims.quote: Data Owner/Admin - This user will enable your source for data policy enforcement in Microsoft Purview for Azure and Amazon S3 sources.

claims.where: Risk assessment: Security & identity; Governance controls: first paragraph
claims.claim: A data source administrator is the role needed to enable Data policy enforcement.
claims.quote: To enable Data policy enforcement, you must have both specific Identity and Access Management (IAM) privileges on the resource as well as specific Microsoft Purview privileges
claims.fix: Replace the enforcement-role clause in both places with: 'Enabling Data policy enforcement requires the Microsoft Purview Data source admin role for the collection or an inheritable parent collection, plus either IAM Owner or both IAM Contributor and IAM User Access Administrator on the resource ARM path or an ancestor.' Cite https://learn.microsoft.com/purview/legacy/how-to-enable-data-policy-enforcement and add that URL to sources. Do not change the separate registration-role statement.

claims.where: Why it matters: meter counts assets; Cost and licensing: Counting assets
claims.claim: An asset in an in-scope location counts whether or not it matches the protection policy's conditions.
claims.quote: The asset doesn't have to match a policy's conditions to be counted, it just has to be in a location that's in the scope of a policy.
claims.fix: Qualify the two asset-count statements with: 'The billing page's general counting rule includes assets that do not match conditions, but its protection-policy example counts only the 50 Confidential-labeled tables out of 100. Confirm the effective billable scope before budgeting.' Both passages are at https://learn.microsoft.com/purview/purview-billing-models#counting-assets; do not silently resolve this inconsistency.

claims.where: Cost and licensing: asset deduplication
claims.claim: An asset counts once regardless of how many policies cover it.
claims.quote: An asset is only counted once, regardless of how many solutions or protection policies cover it.

claims.where: Cost and licensing; Governance guidance: Before rollout
claims.claim: Pay-as-you-go billing requires associating the Microsoft 365 tenant with an active Azure subscription.
claims.quote: The billing mechanisms are Azure based, so you must associate your Microsoft 365 tenant with an active Azure subscription.

claims.where: Cost and licensing; rationale: cost
claims.claim: Pay-as-you-go charges appear in an Azure bill generated at month end.

claims.where: front matter: licensing.notes; Cost and licensing: pricing pointer

Make licensing.notes use the same wording. The link was read, but the pricing destination could not be opened in this run, so a currently published feature-specific rate was not independently verified.

claims.where: front matter: defaultState; summary; Why it matters
claims.claim: This new control is admin-opt-in: enforcement requires an administrator to configure and enable a protection policy.
claims.quote: After you enable these policies, access control is automatically imposed whenever Information Protection detects sensitive information.

claims.where: front matter: risk; rationale: risk
claims.claim: The medium risk rating is justified by mistakes in an administrator-configured allow-list.
claims.quote: defaultState: "admin-opt-in"; summary: "Nothing changes until an admin sets one up."; rationale: "Medium. ... a wrong allow-list or a missed scanner account can block people and scans."
claims.fix: Set risk to low and replace the rationale with: 'Low. This new control restricts nothing until an administrator configures and enables a protection policy; existing behaviour continues if nobody acts.' The assessment scale rates the unconfigured default of a new control, not misconfiguration after opting in.

claims.where: Governance guidance: Before rollout, assigning roles; Governance controls table
claims.claim: Every control the governance checklist asks administrators to configure appears in the controls table.
claims.quote: Before rollout: "Assign the Information Protection and Data Map reader roles to the admins who will author policies"; the controls table covers policies, enforcement, label scope and usage, not role assignment.
claims.fix: The Before rollout role-assignment step has no corresponding controls-table row. Keep this as a coverage limitation; do not add a control row as part of this correction.
